items.stem: A nurse is preparing to renew a nursing license. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Retake the NCLEX at every routine renewal because re-examination is a universal renewal requirement.
options.B: Verify the current renewal requirements of the licensing jurisdiction because continuing-competency, education, and other requirements vary by jurisdiction.
options.C: Use the renewal requirements from the state of original licensure even when the active license is issued by another jurisdiction.
options.D: Assume the license remains active indefinitely unless the employer requests a renewal.

items.rationale: Licensure renewal is governed by the applicable board of nursing. NCSBN recognizes renewal as a licensure process across jurisdictions, but specific renewal requirements vary; the nurse should verify the current requirements of the licensing jurisdiction rather than assume a universal CE rule.
items.locator: Licensure and renewal are governed by the applicable nursing regulatory body; requirements are jurisdiction-specific.

items.stem: Which statement best describes nursing peer review?

options.A: Peer review is the manager’s annual employment-performance appraisal of a nurse’s attendance, goals, and job performance.
options.B: Peer review is informal feedback between coworkers that is not intended to assess practice against professional standards.
options.C: Nursing peer review is a systematic assessment by nursing peers of the quality and appropriateness of nursing care against professional standards.
options.D: Peer review is the credentialing process used to verify an applicant’s initial education and licensure before employment.

items.rationale: ANA describes nursing peer review as a systematic assessment by practicing registered nurses of the quality of nursing care provided by peers against professional standards. It is intended to support accountability, learning, and practice improvement rather than function as a purely punitive process.

items.stem: A charge nurse is determining the appropriate RN, LPN/LVN, and assistive-personnel mix for a shift. Which factors should drive the staffing decision?

options.A: Base the staffing mix primarily on staff seniority because competency differences are addressed after assignments are made.
options.B: Use the same staffing pattern throughout the shift even when patient acuity and required competencies change.
options.C: Base assignments primarily on staff scheduling preferences when the planned head count has been met.
options.D: Base the staffing mix on patient care needs and acuity together with staff scope, education, skills, competencies, and relevant unit factors.

items.rationale: ANA staffing principles emphasize matching staffing resources to patient needs and considering patient acuity, skill mix, education, competencies, unit variables, and changing care demands. A fixed or seniority-only approach does not address safe staffing requirements.
items.source_name: American Nurses Association — Principles for Nurse Staffing
items.locator: Staffing decisions incorporate patient needs, acuity, competencies, skill mix, and practice-setting factors

items.stem: Which statement about nursing documentation is correct?

options.A: Document assessments and care accurately, objectively, and promptly, and correct errors through the approved traceable record process.
options.B: Document planned interventions before they are performed when the nurse expects to complete them by the end of the shift.
options.C: Delete an inaccurate electronic entry so the original information is no longer visible in the record.
options.D: Limit documentation to medications and procedures because patient responses are not part of the legal health record.

items.rationale: NCBI Nursing Fundamentals identifies EHR documentation as a legal document and states that entries should be objective, factual, accurate, and timely. Care not completed must not be charted as completed, and errors should be corrected using an appropriate traceable process rather than erased or concealed.
items.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Fundamentals: Legal Documentation
items.locator: EHR documentation is a legal document; entries must be accurate and timely

items.stem: A medication error is intercepted before it reaches the client. Why is reporting this near miss useful for patient safety?

options.A: A near miss confirms that existing safety controls are adequate, so additional review can distort performance data.
options.B: Reporting the near miss can reveal contributing factors and system weaknesses before a similar event causes patient harm.
options.C: Near misses are useful mainly for identifying which individual should be disciplined when no patient harm occurred.
options.D: Safety reporting should be limited to events that cause injury because no learning can come from intercepted errors.

items.rationale: AHRQ defines a near miss as an error that could have caused harm under different circumstances but was intercepted or did not harm the patient. Patient-safety reporting systems collect near misses so they can be analyzed along with other safety events and used to identify contributing factors and improvement opportunities.
items.source_name: AHRQ — Patient Safety Event Reporting / Near-Miss Terminology
items.locator: Near misses are reportable safety events and can be analyzed for contributing factors

items.stem: A patient, family, and healthcare team disagree about the ethically appropriate treatment plan in a complex case. Which resource is appropriate?

options.A: Request risk management to determine which party is legally liable before the treatment values and goals are clarified.
options.B: Request a routine discharge-planning conference even though the unresolved issue is an ethical conflict about treatment.
options.C: Request a healthcare ethics consultation to help clarify values, options, and ethically supportable approaches to the disagreement.
options.D: Request security to resolve the disagreement because treatment-value conflicts are primarily behavioral-management problems.

items.rationale: The VA National Center for Ethics in Health Care describes ethics consultation as a resource for uncertainty or conflict about what should be done in healthcare. Ethics consultants work with patients, families, and staff to clarify options and help resolve ethically difficult concerns; they are not misconduct investigators.

items.locator: Ethics consultation is a resource for uncertainty or conflict about what should be done in health care and helps clarify ethically supportable options.

items.stem: Which behavior best reflects cultural humility in nursing practice?

options.A: Apply a previously learned cultural profile to predict the patient’s preferences without asking about individual differences.
options.B: Avoid discussing culture or bias so the nurse’s own values cannot influence the interaction.
options.C: Treat completion of cultural-competence training as permanent mastery of the beliefs of patients from that group.
options.D: Use ongoing self-reflection about bias, power, and assumptions while learning from the individual patient’s experiences, values, and preferences.

items.rationale: HHS's CLAS in Nursing program explicitly includes cultural humility and emphasizes self-awareness of beliefs and values as well as privilege, power, bias, and stereotypes, together with learning the patient's cultural identity and responding to the patient's experiences, values, beliefs, and preferences.
items.source_name: HHS Think Cultural Health — CLAS in Nursing
items.locator: Cultural humility includes self-awareness, attention to power and bias, and patient-centered learning

items.stem: Which cluster of findings is most consistent with hyperthyroidism?

options.A: Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, and a rapid or irregular heartbeat.
options.B: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and a slowed heart rate.
options.C: Central weight gain, rounded face, purple striae, and proximal muscle weakness.
options.D: Weight loss, hyperpigmentation, salt craving, and persistent hypotension.

items.rationale: NIDDK lists weight loss despite increased appetite, rapid or irregular heartbeat, sweating or heat intolerance, and other hypermetabolic symptoms among common manifestations of hyperthyroidism. The keyed response best matches this pattern.

items.stem: Which physical finding is most consistent with Cushing syndrome rather than primary adrenal insufficiency?

options.A: Diffuse hyperpigmentation with weight loss, salt craving, and persistent hypotension.
options.B: A rounded face with upper-body weight gain and increased fat over the upper back.
options.C: Enlarged hands and jaw with coarse facial features and increased shoe size.
options.D: Cold intolerance, bradycardia, constipation, and generalized weight gain.

items.rationale: Cushing syndrome commonly causes upper-body weight gain, a rounded face, and increased fat over the upper back and above the collarbones. Weight loss, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, and salt craving are more characteristic of primary adrenal insufficiency.
items.locator: Symptoms and physical changes: upper-body weight gain, rounded face, and fat accumulation around neck/upper back.

items.stem: Which laboratory and fluid-balance pattern is most consistent with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD)?

options.A: Free-water loss with hypernatremia and persistently dilute urine.
options.B: Isotonic volume depletion with hypernatremia and maximally concentrated urine from appropriate vasopressin release.
options.C: Water retention with hypotonic hyponatremia and urine that remains inappropriately concentrated.
options.D: Hypertonic hyponatremia with maximally dilute urine caused by complete suppression of vasopressin.

items.rationale: In SIAD, inappropriate vasopressin activity increases renal water reabsorption, producing water retention, dilutional hypotonic hyponatremia, and urine that is not maximally dilute. This contrasts with diabetes insipidus, which causes free-water loss and dilute urine.
